title: Floating-point equality
question: In a language whose floating-point numbers are standard binary doubles (IEEE 754), what does the expression 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluate to?
options: true, but only when the values are stored in variables
It raises an error when comparing computed floats
true, because results are rounded to 15 digits first
false, because neither 0.1 nor 0.2 is exact in binary
explanation: Binary floating-point builds fractions from powers of two, and decimal fractions like 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so 0.1 + 0.2 yields 0.30000000000000004. The comparison does not silently round to 15 digits, and comparing floats is never an error. Compare with a tolerance (|a - b| < epsilon) or use a decimal type when exact decimal arithmetic matters.

title: Value-type assignment copies
question:
Point is a value type (like a struct), not a reference type, with a field x:

a ← Point(x = 1)
b ← a
b.x ← 5
print(a.x)

What is printed?
options: An error, because value types are immutable
explanation: Assigning a value type copies the whole value, so b is an independent copy and changing b.x leaves a.x untouched. If Point were a reference type (a class instance), a and b would refer to the same object and 5 would be printed. Value types are only immutable when they are declared that way.

title: Silent integer overflow
question:
A counter is a 32-bit signed two's-complement integer, and the language performs no overflow check, so arithmetic wraps around. x starts at 2147483647, the largest 32-bit signed value:

x ← x + 1

What is the value of x afterwards?
options: 2147483647, because the value saturates at the maximum
-2147483648, the smallest 32-bit signed value
2147483648, because x is widened to 64 bits
0, because the counter wraps back to zero
explanation: In two's complement, 2147483647 is 0111...1; adding 1 gives 1000...0, the bit pattern of -2147483648, so unchecked arithmetic wraps from the maximum to the minimum. Saturating at the maximum is a different, explicit kind of arithmetic, the variable's type never widens on its own, and wrapping to 0 is what an unsigned counter does after its maximum. Languages differ by default (wrap, throw, or undefined behaviour), so use a wider type or checked arithmetic when overflow is possible.

title: Passing a list to a function
question:
A list variable holds a reference to a list object, and arguments are passed by value, so the function receives a copy of that reference. What is printed?

function f(lst)
    append(lst, 4)
    lst ← [9]

a ← [1, 2, 3]
f(a)
print(a)
explanation: lst starts as a copy of the reference held by a, so both point to the same list and append mutates the caller's list. Assigning a new list to lst only changes the function's local copy of the reference and does not affect a. Hence a ends up as [1, 2, 3, 4], not [9] and not unchanged. This model, often called call by sharing, is how many mainstream languages pass objects.

title: Missing base case
options: It returns 0, because the calls stop once n reaches 0
It returns 120, because fact(1) multiplies by 1 and stops
It keeps calling itself until the call stack overflows
It loops forever without ever using any extra memory
explanation: Without a base case nothing stops the recursion: fact(5) calls fact(4), ..., fact(0), fact(-1) and so on. Reaching 1 or 0 only changes the value being multiplied; it does not end the calls. Each pending call keeps a frame on the call stack because its multiplication still has to run, so memory grows until the runtime reports a stack overflow (or a recursion-depth error). A base case such as "if n <= 1 then return 1" fixes it.

title: Naive recursive Fibonacci
options: Exponential; memoize fib(k) so each value is computed once
Linear; the slowness comes from the overhead of every call
O(n log n); give the program a larger call stack to use
Quadratic; turn it into a loop to bring it down to linear
explanation: Each call spawns two more and the same subproblems are recomputed over and over, so the number of calls grows roughly like phi^n (about 1.6^n). Memoizing, that is storing each fib(k) the first time it is computed and reusing it, makes the run time O(n). Call overhead is only a constant factor, and a larger call stack allows deeper recursion but the depth here is just n, so it does nothing for speed.

title: Bounding quicksort stack depth
question: An in-place recursive quicksort crashes with a stack overflow on adversarial input. Without changing pivot selection, which change guarantees O(log n) stack depth?
options: Recurse into the larger partition first and the smaller one second
Recurse into the smaller partition and loop (iterate) over the larger one
Switch the recursion from pre-order to post-order
Allocate the partitions on the heap instead of sorting in place
explanation: If you always recurse on the smaller side, each nested call handles at most half the elements, so depth is bounded by log2(n); the larger side is handled by the loop without adding frames. The worst-case time stays O(n^2), but the stack can no longer blow up. Changing order of the two recursive calls or copying data does not bound depth.

title: Dangling pointers
question: What is a dangling pointer (or dangling reference)?
options: A pointer that has been set to null after use
A pointer to memory allocated on the heap rather than on the stack
A pointer whose type does not match the pointed-to value
A pointer that still refers to memory that has already been freed
explanation: A dangling pointer outlives the object it pointed to, for example after that memory is explicitly freed or when a function returns the address of its own local variable; dereferencing it is a use-after-free bug with undefined results. A null pointer is a known-invalid value, not dangling. Memory-safe languages rule dangling references out with garbage collection or with compile-time lifetime checks.

title: Memory leaks in a garbage-collected runtime
question: A long-running web service written in a garbage-collected language grows in memory steadily until it is restarted. Profiling shows millions of objects held by a global (static) dictionary used as a cache with no eviction. Why doesn't the garbage collector free them?
options: They stay reachable from a GC root, so the GC treats them as live
The GC only frees objects that were allocated on the call stack
Objects stored in a dictionary are pinned, never moved or collected
The GC skips all collections while the process is handling requests
explanation: A tracing garbage collector reclaims only objects that are unreachable from roots such as global or static variables, stack variables and handles. A global dictionary is reachable from a root, so everything it references stays alive forever. The fix is bounded caching (size limits and expiration), not forcing collections; the GC does not manage stack memory, does not pin dictionary entries and keeps running under load.

title: Reference cycles with reference counting
question: A runtime manages memory by reference counting alone. A parent node holds strong references to its children and each child holds a strong reference back to its parent. When the last outside reference to the tree is dropped, what happens, and what is the usual fix?
options: The runtime raises an error when it detects the reference cycle
The nodes leak since counts never reach zero; make parent links weak
The compiler rejects the code because counted references can't form cycles
Everything is freed once the root's count drops to zero; no fix needed
explanation: With reference counting, an object is freed only when its count reaches zero; a parent-child cycle keeps every count at least 1, so the memory leaks even though nothing outside can reach it. Plain reference counting neither detects cycles at run time nor rejects them at compile time, and the root's count never drops to zero because its children still reference it. Making the back-references weak breaks the cycle, because weak references do not add to the count.

title: Triangular nested loop
question:
What is the time complexity of this code?

for i from 0 to n - 1
    for j from i to n - 1
        count = count + 1
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
explanation: The inner loop runs n, n-1, ..., 1 times, which sums to n(n+1)/2. Big O drops constant factors and lower-order terms, so this is O(n^2). Starting the inner loop at i halves the work but does not change the growth rate.

title: Binary search step count
question: Roughly how many comparisons does binary search need, at most, to find a value in a sorted array of 1,000,000 elements?
options: About 500,000
About 100
About 1,000
About 20
explanation: Binary search halves the remaining range on each comparison, so it needs about log2(n) steps; log2(1,000,000) is just under 20. 500,000 is the average for linear search, and 1,000 would be sqrt(n). This logarithmic growth is why keeping data sorted pays off when it is searched many times.

title: Amortized dynamic array append
question: A dynamic array (a growable list stored in one contiguous block) doubles its capacity when full, copying all elements to the new block. What is the total cost of appending n items, starting empty?
options: O(n log n) total, because there are log n resizes
O(n^2) total, because each resize copies everything
O(log n) per append, because capacity grows geometrically
O(n) total, so each append is amortized O(1)
explanation: Resizes happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, ..., n, so the copy work is 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n < 2n, plus n writes: O(n) total. Averaged over all appends that is O(1) each, even though an individual append that triggers a resize costs O(n). Growing by a constant amount instead of a factor would make it quadratic.

title: Divide-and-conquer recurrence
question: An algorithm splits its input in half, recursively solves both halves, and merges the results in linear time: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). What is T(n)?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(log n)
explanation: There are log2(n) levels of recursion and each level does O(n) total merge work, giving O(n log n); this is the balanced case of the master theorem and describes merge sort. O(n) would require sub-linear combine work, and O(n^2) would need, for example, quadratic merging or unbalanced splits.

title: Comparison sort lower bound
question: Why can no comparison-based sorting algorithm guarantee better than Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case?
options: A decision tree separating all n! orderings has height >= log2(n!)
Merging two sorted halves always costs exactly n log n comparisons
Each element must be compared with every other element at least once
Memory hierarchy effects add a log n factor to every comparison
explanation: Each comparison has two outcomes, so k comparisons can distinguish at most 2^k input orderings; to separate all n! permutations you need k >= log2(n!) = Theta(n log n) by Stirling's approximation. Comparing every pair would be n^2, which is not required. Non-comparison sorts such as counting or radix sort escape this bound by exploiting key structure.

title: De Morgan's law
question: Which expression is logically equivalent to NOT (isAdmin AND isActive)?
options: (NOT isAdmin) OR (NOT isActive)
(NOT isAdmin) AND (NOT isActive)
NOT (isAdmin OR isActive)
isAdmin OR (NOT isActive)
explanation: De Morgan's law states that NOT (A AND B) equals (NOT A) OR (NOT B): the negation flips the operator and each operand. (NOT isAdmin) AND (NOT isActive) is the negation of an OR, not of an AND. In code, !(a && b) becomes !a || !b, which is handy for simplifying guard clauses.

title: Hexadecimal to decimal
question: What is the decimal value of 0x2F?
explanation: Each hex digit is a power of 16: 2 x 16 + F (15) x 1 = 47. 32 ignores the F digit, and 215 would read 2F as 2*100 + 15. In binary 0x2F is 0010 1111, since each hex digit maps to exactly four bits.

title: Two's complement interpretation
question: A sensor sends the byte 0xFF, which your code reads as a signed 8-bit integer. What value does it hold?
explanation: Signed integers use two's complement: the top bit has weight -128, so 1111 1111 = -128 + 127 = -1. 255 is the unsigned interpretation, -128 is 0x80, and -127 would be the sign-magnitude reading. Mixing signed and unsigned reads of the same byte is a common protocol-parsing bug.

title: Bit trick for powers of two
question: For a positive integer n, what does (n & (n - 1)) == 0 test?
options: Whether n is even
Whether n has its highest bit set
Whether n is one less than a power of two
Whether n is a power of two
explanation: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and all zeros below it, so n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit. The result is zero only when n had exactly one set bit, i.e. it is a power of two. Evenness is tested with n & 1, and all-ones values like 7 would give a non-zero result.

title: Memory hierarchy latency
question: Which ordering goes from lowest to highest access latency?
options: CPU registers, L1 cache, L2 cache, main memory (RAM), SSD
L1 cache, CPU registers, main memory, L2 cache, SSD
CPU registers, main memory, L1 cache, L2 cache, SSD
Main memory, L2 cache, L1 cache, CPU registers, SSD
explanation: Registers are inside the core and accessed within a cycle; L1 takes a few cycles, L2 a dozen or so, RAM on the order of a hundred cycles, and an SSD tens of microseconds. Each level is larger but slower than the one above. Designing for locality keeps data in the faster levels.

title: Little-endian byte order
question: On a little-endian machine such as x86-64, the 32-bit value 0x12345678 is stored at address A. Which byte is at address A?
explanation: Little-endian stores the least significant byte at the lowest address, so memory holds 78 56 34 12. Big-endian (network byte order) would put 0x12 first. When serializing binary data, state the byte order explicitly in the file or protocol format instead of relying on the host's native order.

title: False sharing between threads
question: Two threads each increment their own counter in a tight loop. The counters are adjacent 64-bit integers in the same array, yet throughput is far lower than with one thread. What is the most likely cause?
options: The OS scheduler pins both threads to the same core
The runtime serializes access to elements of one array from different threads
False sharing: both counters share one cache line, bouncing between cores
Integer increments are atomic and take a global memory bus lock
explanation: Cache coherence works at cache-line granularity (typically 64 bytes). When two cores write different variables on the same line, each write invalidates the other core's copy, so the line ping-pongs between caches. Padding or aligning each counter to its own cache line removes the contention; plain increments are not atomic and do not lock the bus.

title: Counting combinations of flags
question: A service has 10 independent boolean feature flags. How many distinct flag configurations are possible?
explanation: Each flag doubles the number of combinations, so there are 2^10 = 1024 configurations, the same as the number of subsets of a 10-element set. 10! = 3,628,800 counts orderings, not on/off choices. This exponential growth is why exhaustive testing of flag combinations quickly becomes infeasible.

title: Pigeonhole principle and hashes
question: You compute a 32-bit hash for each of 5 billion distinct strings. Which statement is guaranteed to be true?
options: Collisions are possible but not guaranteed with a good hash function
No collisions occur if the hash function is cryptographic
Collisions occur only if the strings share a common prefix
At least two strings share the same hash value
explanation: There are only 2^32 (about 4.29 billion) possible hash values, fewer than 5 billion inputs, so by the pigeonhole principle at least two inputs must map to the same value. No hash function quality can avoid this. That is why hash-based structures must always handle collisions with equality checks.

title: Birthday bound for random IDs
question: A system generates uniformly random 64-bit IDs. Approximately how many IDs can be generated before the probability of at least one collision reaches about 50%?
options: About 2^16 (roughly 65 thousand)
About 2^63 (half the ID space)
About 2^48 (roughly 280 trillion)
About 2^32 (roughly 4 billion)
explanation: By the birthday paradox, collisions become likely after about sqrt(N) random draws from N values; for N = 2^64 that is about 1.18 x 2^32. Intuitions based on half the space are wildly optimistic. This is why random identifiers such as UUIDv4 use 122 random bits.

title: Pair with target sum
question: Given an unsorted array of n integers, you must find two values that sum to a target in O(n) time. Which approach works?
options: Sort the array, then binary search for each element's complement
Two nested loops comparing every pair
One pass storing seen values in a hash set and checking for target - x
Recursively split the array in half and combine the results
explanation: With a hash set, each element checks whether its complement was already seen in O(1) on average, so the whole scan is O(n). Nested loops are O(n^2), and sorting plus binary search is O(n log n). Trading memory for time with a hash lookup is one of the most common problem-solving patterns.

title: When greedy fails
question: Coins are [1, 3, 4] and the amount is 6. Greedy (always take the largest coin that fits) picks 4 + 1 + 1. Which technique reliably finds the minimum number of coins for arbitrary coin sets?
options: Greedy, but starting from the smallest coin
Sorting the coins in descending order before running greedy
Binary search over the number of coins
Dynamic programming over amounts 0..6, reusing optimal sub-results
explanation: The optimum here is 3 + 3 (2 coins), which greedy misses because a locally best choice is not globally optimal for this coin system. DP computes best[a] = 1 + min(best[a - c]) for each amount, guaranteeing optimality in O(amount x coins). Re-ordering coins for greedy does not fix the underlying problem.

title: Longest substring without repeats
question: You need the length of the longest substring without repeating characters in a 10 MB log line. Which approach achieves O(n) time?
options: Sort the characters and count runs of distinct values
Generate every substring and check each one for repeats with a set
A sliding window with a map of each character's last index
Recursion that tries removing each character in turn
explanation: The window's right edge advances one character at a time; when a repeat is seen, the left edge jumps past the previous occurrence using the map, so each index moves forward at most n times. Checking all substrings is O(n^2) or worse, and sorting destroys the ordering the problem depends on.

title: Why array indexing is constant time
question: Why is reading arr[i] from a contiguous array O(1)?
options: The address is computed directly as base + i x elementSize
The CPU caches every array element after first access
Arrays are binary-searched by index
The runtime keeps a hash table from indices to elements
explanation: Elements are stored back to back with a fixed size, so the location of element i is a single multiply-and-add from the base address, independent of n. No hashing or searching is involved. Caching helps speed in practice but is not what makes the operation O(1).

title: Many range-sum queries
question: A dashboard issues millions of queries for the sum of values between index l and r on a static array of 1,000,000 numbers. What is the best preparation?
options: Sort the array once so each range can be summed with binary search
Precompute prefix sums, then answer each as prefix[r+1] - prefix[l]
Store the array in a hash set for O(1) lookups
Re-sum the range on each query, since summing a slice is already O(1)
explanation: A prefix-sum array, where prefix[i] holds the sum of the first i values, costs one O(n) pass to build and answers any range sum in O(1). Looping over each range is O(r - l) per query, and sorting or hashing destroys the positional information the query needs. If the array were updated frequently, a Fenwick (binary indexed) tree or a segment tree would be the next step.

title: Writing through an array view
question:
An array a holds [1, 2, 3, 4]. v is a view of a that starts at index 1 and has length 2: it shares a's memory instead of copying it. w is an independent copy of v. The code then runs:

v[1] = 99
w[0] = 50
print(a)

What is printed?
explanation: A view stores a reference to the original memory plus an offset and a length, so v[1] is the same slot as a[1 + 1] = a[2], and writing 99 through v changes a. The copy w owns separate memory, so writing 50 into it leaves a untouched. Forgetting that slices or sub-arrays may share storage with their source is a classic aliasing bug; copy explicitly when the pieces must change independently.

title: UTF-8 encoded length
question: How many bytes does the character 'é' (U+00E9) occupy when encoded in UTF-8?
explanation: UTF-8 uses 1 byte for U+0000..U+007F (ASCII), 2 bytes for U+0080..U+07FF, 3 bytes up to U+FFFF and 4 bytes beyond. U+00E9 falls in the 2-byte range, encoded as C3 A9. That is why byte length and character count differ for non-ASCII text.

title: Insert after a known node
question: You hold a reference to a node in a .NET LinkedList<T> and call AddAfter(node, value). What is the time complexity?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n) amortized
explanation: A doubly linked list only needs to rewire the neighbouring next/previous pointers, so insertion at a known node is O(1). The O(n) cost in linked lists comes from finding the position by walking the list. Arrays, by contrast, must shift every subsequent element.

title: Detecting a cycle in O(1) space
question: You must detect whether a singly linked list has a cycle, using O(1) extra memory. Which technique works?
options: Count nodes until the count exceeds the list's declared size field
Reverse the list and compare it with the original
Move a slow pointer 1 step and a fast one 2; they meet if it loops
Store each visited node in a hash set and check for repeats
explanation: Floyd's tortoise-and-hare algorithm: inside a cycle the fast pointer gains one step per iteration and must eventually land on the slow one; without a cycle it reaches null. A hash set also works but uses O(n) memory. Singly linked lists usually have no reliable stored size to compare against.

title: Linked list versus array traversal
question: Benchmarking shows summing 10 million ints is several times faster in an array than in a linked list, although both are O(n). Why?
options: Arrays are processed in parallel automatically by the CPU
The linked list stores each int as a string
Linked list traversal is actually O(n log n) because of pointer indirection
Arrays are contiguous and cache-friendly; nodes need pointer chasing
explanation: Contiguous arrays exploit spatial locality and hardware prefetching, so whole cache lines of useful data arrive at once. Each list node lives at an arbitrary heap address and its next pointer must be loaded before the next access can start, causing many cache misses. Big O ignores these constant factors, which dominate in practice.

title: Validating brackets
question: Which data structure is the natural fit for checking that brackets like ([{}]) are balanced?
options: A hash set of all bracket characters seen so far
A stack: push openers and pop to match each closer
A min-heap ordered by bracket type
A queue: enqueue openers and dequeue to match each closer
explanation: The most recently opened bracket must be closed first, which is last-in-first-out behaviour. Push each opening bracket, and on each closer pop and verify it matches; the string is valid if the stack is empty at the end. A queue is FIFO and would match the wrong bracket.

title: Choosing a stack in Java
question: In modern Java, which class does the JDK documentation recommend for a single-threaded stack?
options: LinkedList, using add and remove(0)
java.util.Stack, using push and pop
Vector, using add and remove(size() - 1)
ArrayDeque, using push and pop
explanation: ArrayDeque's documentation states it is likely faster than Stack when used as a stack. Stack extends Vector, whose methods are all synchronized, adding needless overhead. LinkedList works but allocates a node per element and is noted as slower than ArrayDeque.

title: Next greater element
question: For each element of an array you need the next element to its right that is larger. Which approach does this in O(n) time?
options: For each element, scan right until a larger element is found
A single pass with a monotonic stack of pending indices
Use a min-heap containing all remaining elements
Sort a copy and binary search for each element's successor
explanation: Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the monotonic-stack scan is O(n) total. When the current value exceeds the top of the stack, it is the answer for that index. Scanning right per element is O(n^2), and sorting loses the 'to the right' positional constraint.

title: Queue operations in Python
question: A Python worker uses a list as a FIFO queue with append() and pop(0). With 1 million pending items it is slow. What is the standard fix?
options: Use collections.deque, with append() and popleft()
Sort the list before each pop(0)
Use a set, since it has O(1) removal
Use list.insert(0, x) with list.pop() instead of pop(0)
explanation: pop(0) on a list shifts every remaining element, costing O(n) per dequeue. collections.deque is designed for fast appends and pops from both ends in O(1). insert(0, x) just moves the O(n) shifting to the enqueue side, and a set has no ordering.

title: Circular buffer full versus empty
question: A fixed-size ring buffer tracks head and tail indices that wrap around modulo capacity. When head == tail, what problem must the design solve?
options: Empty and full look identical; keep a count or leave one slot unused
The indices overflow, so capacity must be a prime number
Elements must be shifted back to index 0
The buffer must be reallocated at double capacity to tell them apart
explanation: After wrapping, head == tail can mean nothing is stored or every slot is filled. Common solutions are tracking a separate size counter or treating the buffer as full when (tail + 1) % capacity == head, sacrificing one slot. Ring buffers never shift elements; that is their main advantage.

title: Hash set versus list lookup
question: You check whether each of 1 million incoming emails is in a blocklist of 100,000 addresses. Why is keeping the blocklist in a hash set much faster than keeping it in a plain list?
options: A hash set keeps the strings sorted for binary search
A hash set stores its data on the stack, avoiding the heap
Membership in a hash set is O(1) on average; in a list it is O(n)
A list compares strings byte by byte; a hash set never compares them
explanation: A hash set hashes the key and inspects a single bucket, so a membership test takes constant time on average, whereas a list must be scanned element by element. Hash sets are unordered, not sorted, and stack versus heap placement is not what makes them fast. After the hashes match, they still compare the candidate keys for equality, to handle collisions.

title: Mutating a key after insertion
question: An order object is added to a hash set, and its hash is computed from its status field. Later, the program changes that same object's status in place. What does a membership test for that same object most likely return?
options: false, as the lookup now goes to a bucket other than where it is stored
An error, since the set refuses lookups of keys changed after insertion
true, since the set recomputes the stored hashes when a field changes
true, since the set holds a reference to that same order object
explanation: The set placed the object in the bucket chosen by its hash at insertion time; the changed status yields a different hash, so the lookup inspects another bucket and misses it, even though the same object is still stored there. A hash table cannot observe field changes and does not rehash on its own. A key must not change in any way that affects its hash or equality while it is stored, so derive hashes from immutable data.

title: Pre-order traversal
question: A binary tree has root 1; 1's children are 2 (left) and 3 (right); 2's children are 4 (left) and 5 (right). What is the pre-order traversal?
explanation: Pre-order visits the node, then its left subtree, then its right subtree: 1, then 2 with 4 and 5, then 3. 4 2 5 1 3 is in-order, 4 5 2 3 1 is post-order, and 1 2 3 4 5 is level-order (breadth-first).

title: Printing a tree level by level
question: You must print an org-chart tree level by level (CEO, then direct reports, then their reports). Which approach fits?
options: Breadth-first traversal using a queue
In-order traversal using recursion
Depth-first traversal using a stack
Sorting nodes by their names
explanation: Breadth-first search visits all nodes at depth d before any node at depth d+1, and a FIFO queue naturally produces that order. Depth-first approaches go deep into one branch first. In-order traversal is defined for binary trees and gives sorted order in a BST, not levels.

title: Why databases use B-trees
question: Why do database indexes such as PostgreSQL's default index use B-trees rather than binary search trees?
options: B-trees avoid storing keys in sorted order, which speeds up inserts
High fan-out keeps the tree shallow, so a lookup touches few disk pages
Binary search trees cannot store duplicate keys
B-trees provide O(1) lookups like hash tables
explanation: Each B-tree node fills a page and holds many keys, so the tree's height is around log base hundreds of n; millions of rows need only 3-4 page reads. A binary tree of the same size would be ~20+ levels deep, each potentially a random I/O. B-trees keep keys sorted, enabling range scans and ORDER BY, and lookups are O(log n), not O(1).

title: In-order traversal of a BST
question: Which traversal of a binary search tree visits the keys in ascending sorted order?
options: Post-order
In-order
Pre-order
Level-order
explanation: In a BST every key in the left subtree is smaller and every key in the right subtree is larger, so visiting left, node, right yields ascending order. Pre-order and post-order emit the root before or after both subtrees, and level-order follows depth, not key order.

title: Inserting sorted keys into a BST
question: Keys 1, 2, 3, ..., 100000 are inserted in order into a plain (non-self-balancing) BST. What is the cost of a lookup afterwards?
options: O(1), because the last key is at the root
O(n log n), because each comparison requires rebalancing
O(n), because the tree degenerates into a linked list
O(log n), because BSTs are always balanced
explanation: Each new key is larger than all previous ones, so it is always attached as the right child; the tree's height becomes n. Search is O(height), hence O(n). Self-balancing trees such as red-black or AVL trees rotate on insert to keep height O(log n).

title: Deleting a node with two children
question: In a BST, how is a node with two children usually deleted while preserving the BST property?
options: Rebuild the tree from an in-order traversal without the key
Copy in its in-order successor, then delete the successor node
Replace it with its left child and discard the right subtree
Remove it and attach both of its children directly to its parent
explanation: The in-order successor is the smallest key in the right subtree, so it is larger than everything on the left and smaller than everything else on the right; copying it in keeps the ordering valid. The successor has at most one child, so removing it is the simple case. A parent cannot adopt two extra children in a binary tree.

title: Ordered map for range queries
question: A Java service stores price levels and frequently needs 'the highest price <= X' and all entries in a price range, with O(log n) updates. Which structure fits best?
options: ArrayList kept sorted, using Collections.binarySearch for updates
TreeMap (a red-black tree), using floorKey() and subMap()
PriorityQueue, using peek() for the highest price
HashMap, iterating over all keys to filter the range
explanation: TreeMap is a self-balancing red-black BST that guarantees O(log n) get/put/remove and supports navigation queries like floorKey and subMap. HashMap has no ordering, a sorted ArrayList makes inserts O(n) due to shifting, and a PriorityQueue only exposes its single top element efficiently.

title: Min-heap operation costs
question: In a binary min-heap with n elements, what are the costs of reading the minimum and removing it?
options: Read O(log n), remove O(log n)
Read O(n), remove O(n)
Read O(1), remove O(log n)
Read O(1), remove O(1)
explanation: The minimum is always at the root (heap[0] in Python's heapq), so reading it is O(1). Removing it moves the last element to the root and sifts it down along one root-to-leaf path, which is O(log n). A heap is not fully sorted, which is why removal cannot be O(1).

title: Top-k from a large stream
question: You need the 100 largest values from a stream of 1 billion numbers that does not fit in memory. What is the efficient approach?
options: A size-100 min-heap, replacing the root when a larger value arrives
Sort the entire stream and take the last 100
Store all values in a hash set, then scan it for the 100 largest
Keep a max-heap of every value seen and pop it 100 times at the end
explanation: A size-k min-heap holds the current top k with the smallest of them at the root; each new value is compared against the root and possibly swapped in with O(log k) work. Total time is O(n log k) and memory O(k). Heaping or sorting everything requires O(n) memory, which is not available.

title: Cost of building a heap
question: What is the time complexity of turning an unordered list of n elements into a binary heap in place with heapify (bottom-up sift-down)?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(log n)
explanation: Most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a few levels; summing heights across all nodes gives a total bounded by about 2n, so bottom-up heapify is linear. Inserting the elements one at a time would be O(n log n). Python's heapq.heapify documents its linear-time behaviour.

title: Equal priorities in a priority queue
question: A .NET job scheduler uses PriorityQueue<Job, int>. Jobs with the same priority are sometimes processed out of submission order. What is the correct fix?
options: Dequeue inside a lock so that submission order is preserved
Switch to PriorityQueue<Job, long> so priorities are more precise
Call EnsureCapacity so the heap does not reorder items
Use a composite priority (priority, sequenceNumber) to break ties
explanation: Binary heaps are not stable: the .NET docs state PriorityQueue does not guarantee first-in-first-out semantics for elements of equal priority. Adding a monotonically increasing sequence number as a tie-breaker yields a total order that respects submission time. Capacity, priority width and locking do not affect heap ordering.

title: Representing a sparse graph
question: A social graph has 10 million users and about 50 million friendships. Which representation is appropriate?
options: A single linked list of all vertices
Adjacency list, using memory proportional to V + E
Adjacency matrix, using memory proportional to V^2
Edge list sorted by weight
explanation: An adjacency matrix for 10 million vertices would need 10^14 cells, almost all empty. An adjacency list stores only the edges that exist, O(V + E), and allows fast iteration over a vertex's neighbours. Matrices are preferable only for dense graphs or when O(1) edge-existence checks dominate.

title: Shortest path in an unweighted graph
question: You need the minimum number of hops between two routers in a network where every link counts equally. Which algorithm is simplest and optimal?
options: Breadth-first search
Dijkstra's algorithm with a Fibonacci heap
Topological sort
Depth-first search
explanation: BFS explores nodes in increasing distance order, so the first time it reaches the target it has found the minimum hop count in O(V + E). DFS finds a path but not necessarily the shortest. Dijkstra works but is unnecessary overhead when all weights are equal, and topological sort applies only to DAGs.

title: Ordering dependent build steps
question: A build tool must run tasks so that each task runs after all its dependencies. Using Python's graphlib.TopologicalSorter, what happens if two tasks depend on each other?
options: A CycleError is raised because no valid ordering exists
The tasks are run in alphabetical order
Both tasks are silently dropped from the ordering
The sorter returns the tasks in insertion order
explanation: A topological order exists only for directed acyclic graphs; a mutual dependency forms a cycle, and graphlib raises graphlib.CycleError when preparing the order. Silently dropping or reordering tasks would hide a real configuration bug. Detecting the cycle lets the tool report it to the user.

title: Dijkstra and negative weights
question: A pricing graph has some edges with negative costs (discounts) but no negative cycles. Why can Dijkstra's algorithm return wrong shortest paths, and what is a correct alternative?
options: Dijkstra loops forever on negative edges; use DFS
Dijkstra requires integer weights; use Floyd-Warshall only for floats
It never re-checks a settled vertex; use Bellman-Ford instead
Dijkstra only works on undirected graphs; use BFS
explanation: Dijkstra's greedy step assumes extending a path never decreases its cost, so once a vertex is settled it is never revisited; a negative edge discovered later can make a cheaper path that it misses. Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V-1 times, handles negative weights in O(VE), and can detect negative cycles. BFS ignores weights entirely.

title: Decrease-key with heapq
question: You implement Dijkstra in Python with heapq, which has no decrease-key operation. What is the standard technique, and its effect on complexity?
options: Search the heap list for the node and edit its distance in place; O(V log V) time
Use a sorted list with bisect.insort; O(log V) per update
Re-heapify the whole list after each relaxation; O(E log V) time
Push duplicate (distance, node) entries and skip stale ones on pop; O(E log V)
explanation: Lazy deletion pushes a duplicate with the improved distance and, when popping, ignores entries whose distance is larger than the recorded best. The heap can hold up to O(E) entries, and since log E <= 2 log V the bound stays O(E log V). Editing in place breaks the heap invariant, re-heapifying costs O(V) per relaxation, and insort is O(V) due to shifting.

title: Data structure for autocomplete
question: Which data structure is designed for quickly finding all stored words that start with a given prefix, such as for search autocomplete?
options: Hash set
Trie (prefix tree)
Min-heap
Circular queue
explanation: In a trie each edge represents a character and each path from the root spells a prefix, so walking the prefix leads to a subtree containing exactly the matching words. A hash set can only test whole keys, and heaps and queues have no notion of prefixes.

title: Trie lookup complexity
question: A trie stores 5 million English words. What dominates the cost of checking whether a word of length L is present?
options: The number of words: O(n) since every word is compared
The word length: O(L), independent of how many words are stored
The number of words: O(log n) like a balanced BST
The alphabet size squared: O(26^2)
explanation: Lookup follows one child pointer per character, so it takes O(L) steps no matter how many words share the trie. A balanced BST of strings would need O(log n) comparisons, each up to O(L). That size-independence is the trie's main advantage for prefix-heavy workloads.

title: Reducing trie memory
question: A trie of long URL paths uses far more memory than the raw strings because most nodes have a single child. Which variant addresses this?
options: Replacing the trie with an adjacency matrix
A radix (Patricia) tree merging single-child chains
A binary heap keyed by URL length
A trie with a fixed 256-entry child array in each node
explanation: Radix/Patricia trees compress runs of single-child nodes into one edge holding a substring, so node count is bounded by the number of keys rather than the number of characters. Fixed 256-entry child arrays make memory worse. Production routers and some databases use radix trees for exactly this reason.

title: Disjoint-set core operations
question: What are the two core operations of a disjoint-set (union-find) data structure?
options: find and union
push and pop
insert and extract-min
enqueue and dequeue
explanation: A disjoint set partitions elements into non-overlapping groups; find returns a set's representative, and union merges two groups. Comparing the representatives of two elements tells you whether they are connected. Push/pop, extract-min and enqueue/dequeue belong to stacks, heaps and queues.

title: Cycle checks in Kruskal's algorithm
question: Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm processes edges by increasing weight and must skip any edge that would create a cycle. Which structure makes that check efficient?
options: A full DFS over the partial tree before adding every edge
A min-heap of vertex degrees
A stack holding the edges added so far
Union-find, skipping edges whose endpoints share a root
explanation: If find(u) == find(v), the endpoints are already connected and the edge would close a cycle; otherwise union(u, v) adds it. With union-find this check is nearly constant time, whereas a DFS per edge would cost O(V) each. The sorting step then dominates, giving O(E log E).

title: Union-find with both optimizations
question: A union-find implementation uses union by rank (or size) together with path compression (or path halving). What is the amortized cost per operation?
options: O(1) worst case for every individual operation
O(sqrt(n)), because paths are halved on each find
O(log n), because ranks bound the tree height
O(alpha(n)), the inverse Ackermann function, effectively constant
explanation: Union by rank alone bounds height to O(log n); combining it with path compression or halving yields Tarjan's amortized O(alpha(n)) bound, where alpha(n) <= 4 for any practical n. Individual operations can still be slower; the guarantee is amortized. SciPy's DisjointSet, for example, uses path halving with union by size.

title: Row-major element offset
question: A matrix with R rows and C columns is stored in a flat array in row-major order. At which index is element (i, j), with zero-based indices?
options: j x R + i
i x R + j
i + j
i x C + j
explanation: Row-major order stores entire rows one after another, so you skip i full rows of C elements and then move j columns: i x C + j. j x R + i is the column-major formula (used by Fortran and NumPy's 'F' order). NumPy and C default to row-major ('C' order).

title: Loop order and cache performance
question: Summing a 10,000 x 10,000 row-major matrix is about 5x faster with for i (rows) { for j (cols) } than with the loops swapped. Why?
options: Column-first loops trigger bounds checks that row-first loops avoid
Row-by-row order lets the compiler skip zero elements
Inner loop over columns reads consecutive addresses, using every byte of each cache line
Swapped loops perform more additions overall
explanation: In row-major storage, consecutive j values are adjacent in memory, so each cache line fetched serves several elements and hardware prefetching works well. Iterating down a column jumps C x elementSize bytes per step, causing a cache miss on nearly every access. The arithmetic performed is identical in both orders.

title: Storing a mostly-empty matrix
question: A recommender builds a 1,000,000 x 100,000 user-item matrix of float64 where only 0.01% of entries are non-zero. What is the right storage choice?
options: A Python dict of dicts keyed by row and column for matrix multiplication
A sparse format such as CSR, storing only non-zero values and their indices
A dense array of float16 to cut memory by 4x
A dense NumPy array, since vectorized operations are faster
explanation: Dense storage would need 10^11 x 8 bytes, about 800 GB; even float16 is 200 GB. CSR stores roughly 10 million non-zeros plus index arrays, a few hundred MB, and supports efficient row slicing and matrix-vector products. A dict of dicts saves memory but is far too slow for linear algebra.
